title: DEMILITARIZATION BY OPEN BURN/OPEN DETONATION (OBOD)
description:
Currently, few closed-disposal alternatives for the demilitarization of bulk energetics and propellants have been proven to meet safety and environmental standards. OB/OD destroys these munitions and explosives in a manner that minimizes risk to the workers, the community and the environment. In addition, this process is compliant with federal or state environmental regulatory requirements for performing Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) - regulated destruction of munitions and explosives. JMC actively manages the military munitions stockpile to safely and securely disable, decontaminate, and demilitarize surplus, obsolete, and inoperable ammunition. (U.S. Army video by Dori Whipple)
The video contains music from a USDA licensed asset from Megatrax.

transcript.text: Ammunition plays a vital role in protecting our nation, but when ammo ages it becomes unstable.
This poses a hazard.
To prevent accidental explosions, surplus, obsolete, and inoperable conventional ammunition stockpiles must be demilitarized and destroyed.

The safe handling and destruction of excess munitions and explosives is coordinated through an enterprise management effort and is achieved by using an environmentally sound and militarization process.
Whereby ammunition is stripped down to its component parts and compounds that are then recycled.
All options for resource recovery and recycling are exhausted prior to declaring munitions as waste.

The logistics of ammunition destruction is challenging. Some munitions items are not able to be treated in this fashion and leave no safe alternative for treatment other than open burning or open detonation.

Open burning is typically used for the destruction of propellants and power technique compositions. This is done in small proportions in metal pans or concrete to prevent round contamination and ensure operational efficiency.
That nation involves the planning and execution of a scheduled detonation by highly trained subject matter experts to deploy an explosion of un-service ammunition.

Department of Defense utilizes demilitarization technologies at military facilities as well as at commercial facilities via demilitarization contracts to reduce the dependency on open burn and open detonation.
Considerations for evaluating alternative technologies depend on the level of risk upon inspection.
For example, carefully stored well-imintoried stockpiles of similar undegrated energetic materials present less risk of accidental detonation versus stress materials.
So to honor Department of Defense's commitment to protect ordinary workers and the public, the handling of unstable energetic materials is kept to a minimum.

Open burn and open detonation destroys these munitions and explosives in a manner that minimizes risk to the workers, the community, and the environment, and is the safest means of munitions destruction.
Currently permitted under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act.
Department of Defense is an industry leader in developing and implementing alternative technologies for demilitarization.
However, alternative technologies require more handling of dangerous explosives, thus increasing risk of injury or death.

Many alternative technologies produce hazardous waste byproducts and require increased energy use, requiring an overall evaluation of the impact to the environment prior to considering the disposal of munitions.
Each of the military services has robust network procedures to assess potential environmental impacts of changes in open burn and open detonation operations.

For more than 30 years, open burn and open detonation units have been evaluated and assessed for environmental risk through permit-mandated multimedia sampling and by conducting human health and ecological risk assessments.
These areas are positioned at locations that are at safe distances from insulation workers in the general population.

They are permitted by the EPA with stringent permitting requirements that regulate quantity and type of munitions that can be processed at each site and have Department of Defense explosive safety board approvals.
There are 34 Department of Defense sites with active open burn and open detonation permits.
The Department of Army was able to reduce the largest number of these permits from 71 in 1988 to 37 in 1998 and currently 18 remaining today.

The Army has also drastically reduced the amount of waste military munitions treated by open burn and open detonation from 14,786 tons in 1998 to a current five-year average of 6,516 tons through the implementation of reused recycling
munitions peculiar equipment and alternative technologies.
To learn more about JMC's Demilitarization Program, Open Burn and Open Debt Nation, please visit www.jmc.army.mil
